stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Marisol Okafor's 2014 novel The Load Line. Dessa, a structural engineer, is visiting a pedestrian bridge she designed twenty years earlier.

Dessa had always told her students that a finished bridge belonged to the people who crossed it, not to the person who drew it. She had believed this, or thought she had. Yet standing at midspan now, she caught herself watching each jogger's stride, waiting for the deck to answer with the slight, calculated give she had once spent a winter computing. When a boy stamped his feet to test it, she felt an absurd urge to thank him. The bridge was theirs, she supposed. But some part of it had never stopped being hers.
choices: To convey that Dessa still feels personally attached to a bridge she says belongs to others
To portray a boy's growing curiosity about how the pedestrian bridge he is crossing was built
To describe the specific calculations Dessa carried out in the winter she designed the bridge
To show that Dessa regrets having taught her students an idea she now believes is plainly false
explanation: The setup puts Dessa at the center. The passage starts with what she has always believed: a bridge belongs to the people who cross it. Then 'Yet' introduces the correction. She watches the deck closely, wants to thank the boy, and ends by admitting that part of the bridge 'had never stopped being hers.' Taken as a whole, the excerpt shows her lasting personal attachment in spite of what she tells her students.

B.why: You moved the focus from Dessa to the boy. He stamps his feet once, and the passage uses that moment to show Dessa's reaction. It says nothing about his curiosity or about how the bridge was built.

C.why: The text says only that Dessa spent a winter computing the deck's give. It never describes the calculations, so you've picked a detail the text doesn't supply.

D.why: Dessa feels torn, not regretful. She still grants that 'the bridge was theirs.' Nothing suggests she now thinks her teaching was false or wishes she hadn't taught it.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Tension between belief that structure belongs to users and continuing personal attachment

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Hollis Arden's 2017 poem "To a First-Year Grower." The speaker addresses a new farmer.

You will want the seed to hurry.
Everyone does. The first spring,
you'll kneel each dawn to check the rows
as if watching could pull green from clay.
It can't. But here is what I learned
from forty harvests of beans and doubt:
the waiting is not wasted. Under you,
the roots are doing arithmetic
you cannot see, and by July
the field will show its work.
choices: To warn a new grower that checking the rows too often will damage the young crop
To lament the many seasons the speaker spent doubting whether the beans would grow
To encourage a new grower to trust that growth is happening even when it is unseen
To explain the process by which bean roots draw nutrients out of heavy clay soil
explanation: The poem speaks to the new grower. It admits that impatience is natural, and then after 'But' comes the real message: 'the waiting is not wasted,' because the roots are working out of sight and 'by July / the field will show its work.' The tone is reassuring, so the purpose is to encourage the grower to trust growth they can't see yet.

A.why: You turned encouragement into a warning. The speaker says watching can't speed the crop up. The poem never says watching harms it.

B.why: 'Forty harvests of beans and doubt' is the speaker's credential, not a lament. The poem looks ahead with hope, so this choice gets the tone backward.

D.why: 'The roots are doing arithmetic' is a metaphor. The poem never explains how roots take up nutrients, so you've credited it with content it doesn't have.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Metaphor of hidden growth happening while observer waits and trusts

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Leland Varga's 2020 novel Fracture Toughness. Imani, a graduate student in materials science, has just watched a ceramic sample she spent months preparing fail a stress test.

The sample broke at less than half the load Imani had predicted, splitting with a sound like a snapped pencil. Dr. Halvorsen was already writing in the lab notebook, murmuring that the fracture pattern was "genuinely interesting." Imani nodded. She knew he meant it kindly, and that he was right: a failure this clean would teach them something. Still, she stood at the press long after he had gone, turning one half over in her gloved hand, unable yet to see it as anything but six months of her life in two pieces.
choices: To show Dr. Halvorsen's excitement about an unexpected result from his laboratory's tests
To portray Imani's lingering disappointment even as she accepts the failure's scientific value
To explain what the fracture pattern revealed about why the ceramic sample broke so early
To suggest that Imani has begun to doubt whether she should remain in materials science
explanation: The setup makes Imani the focus. She agrees that the failure 'would teach them something.' The pivot 'Still,' though, shows she can't yet see the broken sample as anything but lost months. The excerpt captures that mix: she accepts the failure's value while still feeling disappointed.

A.why: This is the trap of shifting to the wrong person. Dr. Halvorsen's interest is there to contrast with Imani's feelings. The excerpt is about her reaction, not his.

C.why: The text calls the fracture pattern 'interesting' but never says what it showed. You've picked a finding the passage doesn't report.

D.why: Imani is disappointed about one sample. Nothing in the text says she is questioning her career, so this choice goes well past the evidence.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Conflict between intellectual acceptance of scientific value and emotional sense of loss

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Oona Maris's 2016 short story "The Eyepiece." Teodor is an amateur astronomer.

For thirty years Teodor had assumed that the point of watching the sky was to find something in it: a new comet, a flaring star, some small light that would carry his name. He had found nothing. Yet on the night his granddaughter first looked through his telescope and gasped at Saturn's rings, rings astronomers had cataloged centuries before she was born, he realized he did not mind. The discovery was hers, and it was enough that he had been the one holding the eyepiece steady.
choices: To portray the granddaughter's ambition to someday discover a new object in the night sky
To describe how Teodor's telescope allowed him to observe fine details of Saturn's rings
To suggest that Teodor feels bitter that astronomers cataloged Saturn's rings long ago
To convey Teodor's realization that his granddaughter's delight fulfills him in a new way
explanation: The story first states Teodor's long-held assumption that watching the sky is about making a discovery of his own. 'Yet' introduces the correction: watching his granddaughter's delight, he finds he doesn't mind that he never found anything, and helping her is 'enough.' The purpose is to convey that realization.

A.why: You moved the focus to the granddaughter. She gasps at Saturn, but the text never mentions any ambition of hers. The excerpt is about what Teodor comes to understand.

B.why: The telescope is only the setting. The passage never describes what the rings look like through it, and this choice ignores Teodor's change of heart, which is the point of the excerpt.

C.why: The text says outright that 'he did not mind.' Mentioning that the rings were cataloged long ago stresses that the discovery was hers, not new. It doesn't express any bitterness.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Recognition that fulfillment shifts from personal achievement to enabling others' joy

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Faris Adeyemi's 2018 novel Aftershock Season. Lucía is a seismologist monitoring a network of sensors after a moderate earthquake.

The readings came in cleanly, each station reporting on schedule, and for an hour Lucía did what she had trained for years to do: she located the epicenter, estimated the magnitude, and sent the bulletin. Her colleagues praised the speed of it. Only when she walked outside and saw her neighbor sweeping broken dishes from his porch did the numbers on her screen become a morning in someone's kitchen. She set down her coffee and went to help him, the bulletin already feeling strangely small.
choices: To show the pride Lucía's colleagues take in how quickly their team issued the bulletin
To explain the procedure seismologists follow to find an epicenter and estimate magnitude
To portray a moment when Lucía's technical view of the quake gives way to its human impact
To suggest that Lucía believes her monitoring work has no real value to her community
explanation: The first sentences show Lucía handling the earthquake as data. The pivot 'Only when' changes that: seeing her neighbor's broken dishes turns 'the numbers on her screen' into something that happened to real people, and she goes to help. The excerpt portrays her shift from a technical view to a human one.

A.why: This is the wrong-person trap. The colleagues' praise gets one sentence, and it sets up the contrast with what Lucía feels afterward. The excerpt is about her.

B.why: The text lists Lucía's tasks but never explains how they're done, and this choice leaves out the turn that the whole excerpt builds toward.

D.why: 'Strangely small' means the bulletin seems minor next to the damage. It doesn't mean she thinks her work is worthless. This choice turns a moment of perspective into a sweeping judgment.

license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Single moment shows how abstract technical work has concrete human consequences

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Ansel Burke's 2021 poem "For the Volunteers Pulling Buckthorn." The speaker addresses people removing an invasive shrub from a forest.

You will not see the oak you're making room for.
Most of you will move away before
the understory fills, before the warblers
find the clearing you made for them.
I know the stems fight back. I know your gloves
tear, and the pile you made looks small
against the hillside's green. Pull anyway.
Some spring you'll never witness,
a trillium will open in the light
your aching hands let in.
choices: To encourage the volunteers to keep working even though they may never see the results
To warn the volunteers that invasive plants will likely return to the cleared hillside
To lament that the volunteers will move away before the restored forest can mature
To explain why buckthorn outcompetes native plants such as oak and trillium on hillsides
explanation: The speaker addresses the volunteers and admits the hard parts: they won't see the oak, the work is exhausting, and the pile looks small. Then comes the key instruction, 'Pull anyway,' along with the promise that a trillium will bloom because of their effort. The poem is encouraging them to keep going even though someone else will see the results.

B.why: You reversed the tone. The poem never says the buckthorn will come back. It ends with native plants thriving, which is hopeful, not a warning.

C.why: The poem does mention that the volunteers will move away, but only as a reason to 'pull anyway.' Reading it as a lament gets the tone wrong.

D.why: The poem names oak and trillium but never explains how buckthorn competes with them. You've read ecological reasoning into it that isn't there.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Encouragement clearly emerges despite detailed emotional obstacles

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Greta Lindqvist's 2008 memoir Leaf Beds. The narrator recalls her first fossil-collecting trip with her father, a paleobotanist.

My father split shale the way other fathers carved roasts, with ceremony and a running commentary. I was nine and had come along mostly for the sandwiches. Then he handed me the hammer, and the slab I struck fell open on a fern frond, every vein intact, pressed there some three hundred million years before anyone had a name for ferns. I did not hear what he said next. I only remember thinking that the rock had been keeping a secret, and that I had been the one it chose to tell.
choices: To portray the father's pride as he watches his daughter uncover her very first fossil
To explain how paleobotanists estimate the age of fern fossils preserved in shale
To show that the narrator decided on this trip to become a paleobotanist herself
To convey the narrator's sense of wonder at the moment she first found a fossil herself
explanation: The memoir centers on the narrator as a child. She starts out uninterested ('mostly for the sandwiches'), then splits open a perfect fern and is so absorbed that she doesn't hear her father. She feels the rock 'chose to tell' her its secret. The excerpt conveys her wonder at that first discovery.

A.why: This is the wrong-person trap. The narrator says she 'did not hear what he said next,' so the text never shows how her father reacted. The focus is on what she felt.

B.why: The text gives an age of about three hundred million years but never says how anyone worked it out. You've credited the excerpt with a method it doesn't describe.

C.why: The moment clearly affected her, but the text never says she decided on a career. This choice adds a consequence the excerpt doesn't give.

license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Narrator's wonder must be distinguished from father's teaching role

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Idris Calloway's 2019 novel The Surveyor's Daughter. In the 1880s, Nell is helping her father complete a map of a river valley.

Each evening Nell inked the day's measurements onto the sheet: the bend where the river doubled back, the ford, the stand of cottonwoods the survey party had camped beneath. A map, her father liked to say, is a promise that a place will stay where you left it. Nell wanted that promise to be true. Yet as the blank spaces filled, she found herself missing them, the way she might miss a question once it had been answered, and she lingered over the last empty corner before she let herself draw it in.
choices: To convey the father's belief that careful mapmaking is the most valuable kind of work
To portray Nell's mixed feelings as the map she is helping create nears completion
To describe the route the survey party followed as it traveled through the river valley
To suggest that Nell leaves part of the map unfinished to preserve the valley's mystery
explanation: Nell is the focus. She wants the map's 'promise' to hold, but after 'Yet' she admits she misses the blank spaces and hesitates over the last corner before filling it in. The excerpt shows her feeling torn as the map nears completion.

A.why: This shifts the focus to the father and overstates his view. He calls a map a promise but never ranks mapmaking above other work, and his saying is there to set up Nell's feelings.

C.why: The bend, the ford, and the cottonwoods are incidental details. The text never lays out a route, and this choice ignores Nell's feelings, which are what the excerpt is about.

D.why: Nell lingers over the last corner, but the text says she does 'draw it in' at the end. She doesn't leave any part of the map unfinished.

license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Ambivalent feelings require understanding mixed values about known versus unknown

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Margery Thale's 1904 novel The Glass Roof. Ida works nights at a small observatory, copying figures for the astronomer Mr. Pell.

For months Ida had thought of the work as nothing more than columns: position, brightness, date, each number set down in Mr. Pell's cramped hand and copied into her own clean one. Tonight, however, he waved her to the eyepiece. The faint smudge she had recorded a hundred times as "nebula, dim" swam up before her, pale and enormous. She stepped back, and for a long while she could not bring herself to pick up her pen.
choices: To convey Mr. Pell's pride in finally showing his assistant a discovery he has been tracking for months
To portray how a single look through the telescope changes Ida's sense of the work she has been doing
To explain how Ida learned to measure the positions and brightness of the objects she records each night
To illustrate Ida's disappointment on finding that the nebula looks far less impressive than her records suggest
explanation: The setup line tells you Ida is the focus. Look at the whole excerpt. At first she thinks of her job as 'nothing more than columns.' After 'however,' she sees the real object behind one of her entries, and it leaves her unable to go back to her pen. So the excerpt shows her view of routine work being transformed by one sight through the telescope. Choice B names the right person and the right change.

A.why: You moved the focus from Ida to Mr. Pell. The text never describes his feelings. All he does is wave her over. It also never says the nebula is his discovery. The excerpt is about Ida's reaction, not his pride.

C.why: You supplied a detail the text never gives. Ida copies figures that are already 'set down in Mr. Pell's cramped hand.' Nothing shows her learning to take measurements herself.

D.why: You reversed the tone. The nebula appears 'pale and enormous,' far more than the 'dim' smudge in her records, and her stunned silence suggests awe, not disappointment.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Ilse Marrow's 2019 novel The Gauge House. Each morning, Dena walks to a stone hut beside the river to record the water level.

When Dena first took the job, the numbers in her ledger had seemed like nothing more than a chore to be finished before breakfast. Yet over the years she had come to read them differently. A rise of two centimeters meant snow melting on hills she had never visited; a sudden drop meant someone upstream had opened the irrigation gates. Standing at the painted pole, she felt the whole valley speaking to her.
choices: To explain how a river's level reveals snowmelt and irrigation upstream
To portray the careless way farmers upstream manage the river's water
To convey Dena's growing frustration with a tedious daily routine
To show how Dena's view of a routine task has deepened over time
explanation: The setup line makes Dena the focus. The passage moves from what she once thought (the readings were 'nothing more than a chore') to 'Yet over the years she had come to read them differently,' and ends with her feeling that 'the whole valley' is speaking to her. Put plainly, the excerpt shows that a dull task has come to feel like a connection to the land around her. Choice D names the right person and the right change.

A.why: You picked something the passage says, not what it's for. The snowmelt and irrigation details are there to show how Dena now reads her numbers. The text isn't trying to teach hydrology, and the passage is really about her change in outlook.

B.why: You moved the focus away from Dena. Someone upstream opening the gates is just one thing she infers from a drop in the water. The text never calls anyone careless, and the excerpt is about her.

C.why: You reversed the direction of the passage. Dena saw the job as a chore only at first. The 'Yet' turns away from that, and by the end she feels the valley speaking to her, which is closer to wonder than frustration.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Rafael Okonjo's 2021 short story "Small Words." Mira, a linguistics student, is recording her grandfather's speech for a study of a fading regional dialect.

Mira had planned to collect vocabulary: the word for a calf born late in the season, the word for the hour before a storm. But her grandfather kept wandering from the list, telling her about the harvest dances, the ferry that no longer ran, the brother who had left for the city. At first she steered him back to her questions. Then she set down her pen and simply listened, realizing that the words she wanted had never existed apart from these stories.
choices: To portray a grandfather's lasting grief over a brother who moved away
To convey Mira's realization that the dialect is bound up with memory
To show how Mira's impatience with digressions undermines her study
To explain which words linguists record when documenting a dialect
explanation: The setup line makes Mira the focus. She arrives with a word list, tries to keep her grandfather on it, and then stops to listen, realizing the words 'had never existed apart from these stories.' The excerpt as a whole leads up to that realization: the language can't be separated from the life and memories it comes from. Choice B states it.

A.why: You switched to the wrong person. The brother who left is one item in the grandfather's list of memories. The text never describes his feelings about it, and the excerpt is built around Mira's realization, not his grief.

C.why: You read only the middle of the passage. Mira does steer him back at first, but then she sets down her pen and listens. Nothing suggests her study suffers. The ending points the other way.

D.why: You claimed more than the excerpt gives. Two sample words from Mira's list don't make a lesson on how linguists work, and the passage is a story about one student's change of mind, not an account of a method.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Halvard Prete's 1998 poem "To a Young Forecaster."

You will be wrong. The sky will change its mind
between your map and morning, and the rain
you promised will go elsewhere. Never mind.
Look up again tomorrow. Look again.
The clouds have fooled the wisest; they will learn
your patience long before you learn their ways.
Keep watching. Every error is a turn
toward the sky you'll read in later days.
choices: To warn a young forecaster that the sky is too unpredictable to forecast
To describe the way clouds shift between the evening map and the morning
To recount a time when the speaker's own forecast of rain proved wrong
To encourage a young forecaster to keep going despite inevitable errors
explanation: The title tells you who the poem is speaking to: a young forecaster. The speaker admits that mistakes will happen ('You will be wrong'), then keeps telling the forecaster to carry on: 'Never mind,' 'Look again,' 'Keep watching.' The poem ends by calling every error 'a turn / toward' future skill. The tone is reassuring and encouraging, which is what choice D says.

A.why: You took the right person but reversed the tone. The poem admits the sky is hard to predict, but it never says forecasting is pointless. It says the opposite: keep looking, and the errors will lead to skill. Encouraging is not the same as warning.

B.why: You picked a detail instead of the purpose. The sky changing 'between your map and morning' is the situation the poem starts from. Its job is to speak to the forecaster, not to explain how clouds behave.

C.why: You added a story the poem doesn't tell. The speaker says 'the wisest' have been fooled but never describes a forecast of their own. The rain that 'will go elsewhere' is the young forecaster's, and it is in the future.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Maren Holt's 2019 novel The Lower Terrace. Ines has joined an archaeological excavation in southern Portugal for the summer.

Ines had always pictured archaeology as a series of revelations: a trowel strikes bronze, someone shouts, a photograph is taken. For her first two weeks on the site, however, she found only soil. She scraped it away in layers thinner than a fingernail, poured it through screens, and wrote numbers on paper bags. Somewhere in the third week she stopped waiting for the shout. She began to notice how the earth changed color one shade at a time, and she found she could read those shades the way her grandmother had once read the sky.
choices: To portray how Ines comes to value the slow, careful work she had not expected the excavation to involve
To describe the particular artifacts Ines uncovers once she learns to read the changing colors of the soil
To convey her grandmother's skill at reading the weather, which Ines has long tried to imitate on the site
To suggest that Ines regrets joining a project that has failed to produce any of the discoveries she hoped for
explanation: The setup line tells you the focus is Ines. The passage opens with what she expected (dramatic finds), turns at 'however' to what she actually does (scraping, sifting, labeling), and ends with her learning to read the soil's shades. Taken as a whole, the excerpt shows her coming to appreciate slow, patient work she hadn't pictured. That is what choice A says.

B.why: The text never says Ines finds any artifacts. What she learns to read is the soil itself. You added a concrete detail the excerpt doesn't give, probably because a dig 'should' end in a find.

C.why: The grandmother shows up only in the last line's comparison. You took an incidental detail and treated it as the excerpt's point. The text also never says Ines has been trying to copy her.

D.why: This gets the turn backwards. Ines stops waiting for the big moment and starts noticing, and even enjoying, the soil's shades. That is a change of heart, not regret.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Ruth Calloway's 2016 novel Second Shift. In 1934, Della works at a cannery where workers are paid a fixed amount for each crate they fill.

For six years Della had believed that the piece rate rewarded speed, and she was fast. She filled more crates than anyone on the line, and every Friday the extra coins in her pay envelope felt like proof. But that spring the rate dropped from four cents a crate to three, and then, in June, to two and a half. Della worked faster still. On the last Friday of the month she counted her envelope twice at the kitchen table and understood that the faster she went, the less each crate was worth.
choices: To convey Della's realization that working faster no longer protects her earnings as the rate keeps falling
To portray Della's pride in being the fastest worker on the cannery line during her first six years there
To explain the reasons the cannery owner gives his workers for lowering the piece rate month after month
To suggest that Della deliberately slows her pace once she learns that the piece rate has been reduced
explanation: The excerpt follows the 'old belief, then the correction' pattern. Della has believed that speed pays. After 'But,' the rate keeps falling, she works even faster, and in the last sentence she understands that her speed is losing value. That realization is what the whole passage builds toward, so choice A is the answer.

B.why: Della's pride in her speed is only the opening setup, the belief the passage goes on to overturn. You picked the first part of the excerpt and missed where it ends up.

C.why: The owner never appears and no reasons are given for the cuts. This choice moves the focus off Della and invents details the text doesn't contain.

D.why: The text says the opposite: 'Della worked faster still.' You may have assumed what a sensible worker would do instead of checking what Della actually does.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Anika Sorel's 2018 poem "To My Son, Before His First Vaccination."

Hold still, small one. The needle is quick,
a bee that does not stay.
What it leaves is not a wound but a lesson:
a faint likeness of a danger,
too weak to harm you, strong enough to study.
Your blood will learn its face
and keep the drawing somewhere deep,
so that if the real thing ever knocks,
you will already know its name
and open no door.
choices: To reassure a child that a brief pain will help his body recognize and resist a later threat
To warn a child that the needle carries a danger his body may not be strong enough to resist
To compare the quick sting of a needle to the sting of a bee that a child once felt in a garden
To identify which illnesses the vaccine guards against and how long the protection will last
explanation: The title tells you the poem is addressed to the speaker's son. She calms him ('Hold still,' 'the needle is quick') and explains that the 'faint likeness of a danger' is 'too weak to harm you.' His blood will remember it, so he can turn away the real threat later. The tone is reassuring, and the point is protection, which matches choice A.

B.why: This flips the tone. The poem calls the likeness 'too weak to harm you' and ends with the child safely opening 'no door.' You read an encouraging poem as a warning.

C.why: The bee is a passing image in the second line, used to show how quick the needle is. You took one comparison for the purpose of the whole poem. The garden memory is never mentioned either.

D.why: The poem never names an illness or says how long protection lasts. You added factual details the text doesn't give, probably because you know what vaccines do rather than what this poem says.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Miriam Okafor's 2009 novel The Last Speaker. Ruth, a linguist, is recording Tessaly, an elderly woman who is one of the few remaining fluent speakers of her village's language.

Tessaly said the word for river again, slowly, so that Ruth could write it down. Ruth wrote it: four letters, neat and correct. But when Tessaly said it a third time, she was smiling, and the word seemed to carry the sound of water over stones, the cold of a morning crossing, the name of someone Ruth would never meet. Ruth looked down at her four letters. They were accurate, she thought, and they were almost nothing.
choices: To convey Ruth's sense that her written record holds far less than Tessaly's spoken word
To portray Tessaly's frustration that Ruth keeps failing to write the word down correctly
To explain how Ruth worked out a spelling system for the sounds of the village's language
To show Tessaly's satisfaction that her language will finally be preserved in written form
explanation: The setup tells you Ruth is the focus. The excerpt sets two things against each other: Ruth's four letters, which are "neat and correct," and the spoken word, which carries water, cold, and a person's name. The last line, "accurate... and almost nothing," names the gap between them. So the text's purpose is to convey Ruth's sense of how much her record leaves out.

B.why: You assumed the repetition meant something was going wrong. The text says Ruth's letters are "neat and correct" and that Tessaly is smiling, so there's no failure and no frustration.

C.why: You read a process into the scene that isn't there. Ruth writes down one word, and the text never describes her designing a spelling system.

D.why: You moved the focus from Ruth to Tessaly and invented a feeling. The excerpt is about Ruth's reaction, and it suggests writing can't preserve the word. It doesn't celebrate that it can.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Hollis Brandt's 1998 poem "To a Young Diver." The speaker addresses a student about to make a first dive on a coral reef.

Up here the water is only a glare,
a flat gray sheet that hides its floor.
Go under. Let the noise of the boat fall away.
Below, the reef is a city that never sleeps:
parrotfish grinding coral into sand,
an octopus folding itself into a crack.
What looks like nothing from the deck
is crowded, busy, alive. Go see it.
choices: To encourage the diver to look past the sea's dull surface to the life beneath it
To warn the diver that the reef holds dangers that cannot be seen from the boat
To describe how parrotfish and octopuses compete with each other for reef space
To convey the speaker's regret at no longer being able to dive on the reef below
explanation: The poem speaks to the diver and sets two views side by side: from the deck the water is "a flat gray sheet" that looks like "nothing," but below it is "crowded, busy, alive." The commands "Go under" and "Go see it" make the tone encouraging. So the purpose is to urge the diver to look past the dull surface to the life underneath.

B.why: You flipped the tone. "Hides its floor" might sound threatening, but what's hidden turns out to be a lively city, and the speaker tells the diver to go and see it. That's encouragement, not a warning.

C.why: You treated two images as the poem's subject and added a relationship the poem never mentions. The parrotfish and octopus are examples of reef life, and nothing says they compete.

D.why: You moved the focus from the diver to the speaker. The poem is addressed to the student, and nothing suggests the speaker can no longer dive or feels regret.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Dolores Vance's 2014 memoir Second Shift. In 1979, the narrator's mother has just started a job at a fish cannery.

My father earned nearly twice what my mother did; everyone at our table knew it, and he mentioned it often. So I was puzzled, that first Friday, by the way she held her pay envelope. She did not open it right away. She set it beside her plate and kept touching its edge through dinner, as if checking that it was still there. Later I understood. The amount was smaller than his. But for the first time in her life, it was hers.
choices: To convey the narrator's mother's quiet pride in earning wages of her own
To portray the narrator's father's pride in earning more than his wife did
To explain why the mother's cannery wages were lower than the father's
To show the narrator's mother's disappointment at how little her job paid
explanation: The setup and most of the excerpt focus on the mother. The text admits the gap between the two wages (his is nearly twice hers), then says that gap isn't what matters to her: "smaller than his... But... it was hers." The way she keeps touching the envelope shows quiet pride in having her own pay.

B.why: You picked the right family but the wrong person. The father's boasting is background in the first sentence. The rest of the excerpt is about the mother's reaction to her own pay.

C.why: You looked for a reason the text never gives. It says her pay was smaller but never explains why, and it gives no details about cannery work or pay rates.

D.why: You focused on the smaller amount and missed the pivot on "But." She handles the envelope with care, as if it were precious, which shows pride, not disappointment.
